preference_rationale:
Both are defensible depending on how strong the retail claim needs to be, which is why this stays weak. Ultimately the point is to understand whether round lots are profitable to trade against; proving statistically that they are retail is a secondary goal. A treats it as secondary and tests it inside the pipeline; B makes it a hard gate and can die on it.

There is no strict order-level disclosure of retail versus institutional to a market maker - on lit venues orders arrive anonymized, and the only genuine tag is a Retail Liquidity Program flag, which has near-perfect precision but very low recall. B accepts this and triangulates imperfect public labels. But this firm internalizes retail flow, so it holds proprietary ground truth on its own book that no outside researcher has, and neither plan reaches for it. That makes B's five-gate apparatus a solution to a data problem this particular firm does not have.

The mechanism and broad-market readings are both partially right, but the payoff question is the primary one. It stays weak because adverse selection is this firm's central risk, and there is a real argument that knowing what you are quoting against matters more here than it would to a daily long-short book.
critique_A:
The horizon is wrong for the question and for this firm. Trading against retail flow is liquidity provision at nanoseconds to seconds; A builds a daily signal with t+1 entry and a five-day hold, which is a different business. A half-notices this in its pitfalls, observing that a one-day sign would be liquidity provision, but the design never follows the observation.

Its practical constraints are the wrong practical constraints. Effective half-spread, square-root impact, borrow fees, participation caps and capacity from $50M to $5B AUM are the binding costs for a daily long-short book, not for a quoting business where the binding constraint is realized spread capture net of adverse selection and whether the classification runs inside the quoting loop.

The round-lot definition is too narrow. 100 shares can be a lot, and the analysis should also consider 1, 5, 10 and 20 shares as round. A explicitly holds the 100-share threshold fixed despite the SEC's tiered redefinition, where B at least computes both fixed-100 and the tiered version.

Structural breaks are part of the experiment and should be accounted for. A handles the December 2013 odd-lot reporting change and the later round-lot tiering, but never addresses the half-penny tick regime, which degrades the sub-penny retail classification that RETOIB is built from - the very control the round-lot filter is residualized against.

Like B, it never reaches for the firm's own internalized flow, which is the one place real retail labels exist.
critique_B:
It makes the secondary question the gate, and the gate rests on labels that cannot be established cleanly. There is no strict order-level retail-versus-institutional disclosure to a market maker, so five conjunctive kill tests against imperfect labels mean a label-quality failure reads as a signal failure and the project dies on the wrong evidence.

Worse, the labels B works so hard to triangulate - Rule 605 reports, RLP flags, sub-penny classification, VandaTrack - are the toolkit of a researcher with only public data. This firm internalizes retail flow and therefore has proprietary ground truth on its own book. B could settle G1 through G4 directly off that flow with real labels instead of latent-class estimation, and never considers it. The evidence standard is calibrated to a poorer setting than the one it is in.

B handles the half-penny break by truncating the sample to the months before the compliance date rather than accounting for it. Structural breaks are part of the experiment and should be modelled, not avoided by shortening the window.

It carries the same horizon error as A: Phase 2 is decile sorts and Fama-MacBeth at daily frequency, when the question is a market-making one operating at nanoseconds to seconds.

All of the economics is deferred to a Phase 2 that only happens if all five gates pass.
why_loser_was_defensible: A more conservative firm would take method B's view, wanting more confidence that round lots are connected to dumb money before deciding whether they are profitable to trade against. A more aggressive firm lets the P&L speak, does not much care whether the flow is retail, and takes on the adverse-selection risk. Which is right depends on how strong the retail claim needs to be, and that is a question about firm posture rather than about method. For a market maker the conservative reading has real force, since quoting into informed flow you had labelled uninformed is precisely the way this business loses money.
